Listen to this article Share At seven in the evening, the office is still lit. Employees revise presentations, answer emails, and wait for approvals. The managing director sees dedication. But the same scene may reveal an expensive failure: an organisation consuming its people’s energy without making sufficient progress. Somewhere, a customer is waiting for a decision that no one feels authorised to make. Before celebrating the long hours, leadership should ask what made them necessary. This question holds significant importance for Nigerian businesses. Operating difficulties can absorb management attention and narrow the room for error. These pressures deserve serious acknowledgement. Yet they also increase the cost of internal waste. Every avoidable delay consumes resources already stretched by circumstances beyond the company’s control. The discipline is to distinguish unavoidable difficulty from dysfunction that has become familiar. Consider a company where a modest customer refund requires five signatures. Each manager handles the request diligently. Each department records its contribution. Two weeks later, the customer receives money that could have been returned in an afternoon. The paperwork demonstrates compliance. The experience demonstrates failure. “Performance measurement demands the same courage. A sales team can reach its target through discounts that erode profitability. Procurement can secure cheaper materials that cause expensive production failures. Customer service can close complaints promptly without resolving them. Everyone has likely been busy. The process itself has made poor service the predictable outcome of conscientious work. This is where the pursuit of excellence must begin: by examining how work actually gets done. Which approvals protect the organisation? Which exist because a senior executive once demanded them? Which reports inform decisions, and which are produced because somebody produced them last month? These questions can unsettle powerful people. An approval is sometimes more than a control; it is a daily affirmation of status. Removing it requires leaders to value institutional effectiveness above the reassurance of being consulted. Performance measurement demands the same courage. A sales team can reach its target through discounts that erode profitability. Procurement can secure cheaper materials that cause expensive production failures. Customer service can close complaints promptly without resolving them. The figures may be accurate, but the picture they present may be misleading. Customers experience the consequences across departmental boundaries. They do not care that procurement met its savings target if the product fails. Leaders must therefore examine how one unit’s apparent success affects the rest of the business. Otherwise, the organisation rewards people for transferring problems rather than solving them. People development is equally vulnerable to appearances. Workshop attendance proves that training occurred; it says little about whether capability improved. The meaningful questions arise afterwards. Can employees now exercise better judgement? Can they resolve problems they previously escalated? Have they acquired the authority and tools to use what they learned? A manager who must intervene in every decision may appear indispensable. That dependence may also reveal how little capacity the manager has built. Nor should permanent overwork be mistaken for commitment. An occasional late night may reflect an exceptional demand. Repeated late nights warrant scrutiny of workloads, staffing and priorities. An organisation that relies on exhaustion to meet ordinary obligations is drawing down capacity it has not learned to replenish. Technology can deepen these weaknesses when management purchases systems without reconsidering processes. Imagine introducing a digital platform while retaining the paper approvals it was intended to replace. Employees now serve two procedures. The investment has modernised the appearance of work while increasing its burden. The decisive question should precede the purchase: what specific obstacle will disappear? Frontline employees can help answer it. They know where information stalls, where customers become frustrated and where a supposedly straightforward procedure repeatedly breaks down. Their candour, however, depends on what happens when they speak. Accountability becomes hollow when executives demand ownership but punish unwelcome information. Employees learn to protect themselves through silence, excessive email copying, and repeated requests for permission. Management then mistakes the defensive behaviour it has encouraged for a lack of initiative. Credible accountability sets clear expectations, provides reasonable support, and evaluates results fairly. It distinguishes negligence from a considered decision that did not succeed. Above all, it reaches upwards. Boards must scrutinise executive judgement as seriously as executives scrutinise employee performance. Individual responsibility remains essential. Employees owe their organisations competence, honesty and care. Leadership’s responsibility is to create conditions in which those qualities can produce results. Return, then, to the office at seven in the evening. The lights alone tell us very little. Better questions concern what customers received, what decisions moved forward, and whether tomorrow’s work will be easier because of something learned today. Excellence becomes credible when good performance can be repeated without extraordinary personal sacrifice. Until then, the late departure may be less a badge of honour than a question management has avoided answering. Dr Dakuku Peterside is a management and leadership turnaround expert.
